Physics Lab 1

Wrecking Ball

Build a chain and a ball, give them physics, and let gravity demolish a wall in Blender.

Start the lab

Rendered in Blender by following the steps in this lab.

Today

We are learning

how a physics engine moves things for you: you build a chain and a wall, tell Blender which parts are heavy, which are fixed and which are joined, and let gravity make the animation.

You need Blender 4.2 or newer and a mouse with a scroll wheel (laptop trackpad? see this fix). This lab takes about two lessons. Save your file as PhysicsLab1_WreckingBall_YourName.blend.

You’ve got it when you can

  • turn a torus into a chain link in Edit Mode
  • add Rigid Body physics and choose Active, Passive and a collision shape
  • copy a link with exact offsets and turns so a chain interlocks
  • rotate a group around a pivot with the 3D cursor
  • join rigid bodies with Point constraints so the chain holds
  • bake a simulation and render it as an .mp4

The plan

Six parts. Each one ends with a picture of what your scene should look like.

  1. Part 1One chain linkSteps 1–4
  2. Part 2Physics, then the chainSteps 5–8
  3. Part 3The ballSteps 9–11
  4. Part 4Ground and wallSteps 12–14
  5. Part 5Raise, join, swingSteps 15–18
  6. Part 6Camera, bake, renderSteps 19–22

You set it up, physics does the acting

In the car lab you keyframed every movement. Here you keyframe nothing. You give each object a type (Active things fall and bounce, Passive things never move), a shape for collisions, a mass, and some joints. Then you press Space and Blender’s physics engine works out every frame.

The trick is in the setup. A chain only hangs if something Passive holds its top. Links only stay together if joints connect them. A wrecking ball only swings if it starts raised. And a simulation is only repeatable if you bake it before you render.

Word bank — open this if a word in the steps is new
Rigid body
An object the physics engine moves as one solid piece: it falls, bounces and collides, but never bends.
Active / Passive
Active bodies move. Passive bodies never move but things collide with them (the ground, the anchor).
Animated
A Passive body that follows keyframes you set, and still pushes things. Not used in this lab.
Collision shape
The simple shape the engine uses for collisions: Box, Sphere, Convex Hull (shrink-wrap, holes filled) or Mesh (exact).
Mass
How heavy, in kilograms. Heavier things push lighter things around.
Constraint (joint)
A connection between two rigid bodies. A Point constraint is a ball joint: they swing freely but cannot pull apart.
Pivot point
What a rotation turns around. Median Point is the middle of the selection; 3D Cursor is wherever the cursor is.
3D cursor
The red-and-white ring. New objects appear there, and it can be the pivot. Shift+S moves it; Shift+C sends it home.
X-ray
See-through viewport (Alt+Z). Box select then reaches hidden vertices too.
Origin
The orange dot an object is placed, rotated and jointed by. Origin to Geometry puts it in the middle.
Cache
Blender’s memory of simulated frames. Playing fills it; changing anything empties it.
Bake
Simulate every frame and lock the cache so scrubbing is instant and the render matches.
Substeps / iterations
How carefully the engine works each frame. The defaults (10 and 10) are fine for this scene.

Part 1

One chain link

Tools: Add › Mesh › Torus, the sidebar, Edit Mode with X-ray, Set Origin.

The whole chain is copies of one link, so the link is made carefully once. A torus is a ring; stood up and stretched it is a chain link. Its origin goes in the middle so the joints land in the right place later.

How the steps work

Each step has a Where line (which part of the Blender window to look at), a Watch animation of the mouse doing the step (pause it, drag the slider, or use the arrow buttons to go one move at a time), and a Do this list of the same moves as a, b, c. Do one move, look at the animation, do the next. The drawings are simplified, not screenshots: the words and positions match Blender, the exact colours and spacing may not.

  1. Start fresh and save

    Layout workspace › the File menu at the very top-left.

    Do this:

    1. a
      File › New › General. You get a cube, a camera and a light.
    2. b
      Click the cube once (orange outline), press X and click Delete. Keep the camera and the light.
    3. c
      File › Save As. Make a folder called Physics labs, type PhysicsLab1_WreckingBall_YourName and click Save Blender File.

    You should now see: the window title shows your file name, and the Outliner (top right) lists only Camera and Light.

    Why save before doing anything?

    Physics simulations are stored in a cache next to the file. In an unsaved file Blender keeps the cache in memory only, and some cache options are greyed out. Save first and everything works.

  2. A ring, stood up

    The Add menu, then the sidebar (N).

    Do this:

    1. a
      Front view: click the hollow green circle on the gizmo or press Numpad 1.
    2. b
      Add › Mesh › Torus. A ring appears at the centre. From the front it looks like a flat bar, because it is lying down like a plate.
    3. c
      Press N for the sidebar. In Rotation, X: 90, Enter.

    You should now see: a standing ring facing you, 2.5 m across, with an orange outline. The sidebar shows Rotation X 90°, Y 0°, Z 0°.

    Why 90 around X?

    The X axis runs left-right across your screen in Front view. Turning the ring 90° around that axis tips it from lying flat to standing up, like lifting a plate onto its edge toward you.

  3. Stretch it into a link

    The viewport, in Edit Mode.

    Predict first: If you forget X-ray and box-select the top half, how many of the vertices at the back of the tube get selected?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport. Tab: Edit Mode. The ring turns into dots (vertices).
    2. b
      Alt+Z: X-ray on. The ring goes see-through. Now a box selects the dots at the back as well as the front.
    3. c
      Drag a box from above the ring, left of it, down to just above its middle line and across to the right. Everything in the top half turns orange.
    4. d
      G, then Z, type 1, Enter. The top half moves up 1 m. The ring is now an oval, 3.5 m tall.
    5. e
      Alt+Z (X-ray off), Tab (back to Object Mode). Right-click the link › Shade Smooth.

    You should now see: a smooth oval link, 2.5 m wide and 3.5 m tall, with straight sides.

    What if the box selects too much or too little?

    Click an empty spot in the viewport to deselect everything and drag the box again. The line to aim for is the ring’s middle: everything above it, nothing below. A few extra dots near the middle do not matter.

  4. Origin in the middle, 18 m up, named Link

    The Object menu, the sidebar, F2.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Object › Set Origin › Origin to Geometry. The orange origin dot jumps from where the round ring was to the middle of the oval.
    2. b
      Sidebar Location Z: 18, Enter. The link flies up out of view; scroll the mouse wheel to zoom out until you see it.
    3. c
      F2, type Link, Enter.

    You should now see: a link high above the red ground line, origin dot in its middle, named Link in the Outliner.

    Why does the origin matter so much?

    In Step 17 Blender puts each joint half-way between two neighbouring links’ origins. With the origin in the middle of each link, that half-way point is exactly where the two links touch. With the origin off-centre the joints land inside the metal and the chain jerks.

End of Part 1. Save.

Part 2

Physics, then the chain

Tools: the Physics tab, Shift+D, R Z.

Rigid Body is added to the one link first, because copies carry their physics with them. Then the link is copied down five times, each copy turned a quarter turn so the chain interlocks. The top link becomes Passive: the hook that holds everything up.

Collision shape explorer

Pick an object and a shape. The blue outline is what the physics engine really collides.

  1. Rigid Body on the link

    Properties editor › the Physics tab (blue orbit icon, near the bottom of the tab column).

    Do this:

    1. a
      With Link selected, click the Physics tab.
    2. b
      Click Rigid Body. A Rigid Body panel appears. Type stays Active.
    3. c
      Mass: 2, Enter. Leave Shape on Convex Hull.

    You should now see: the Rigid Body button now has an × on it, and the panel reads Type Active, Mass 2 kg, Shape Convex Hull.

    Why not Mesh, like the old lab said?

    Mesh is the exact ring, hole and all, so links could interlock for real. In practice Blender fights to keep thin tubes apart and the chain explodes or picks up energy from nowhere. The joints in Step 17 hold the chain instead, and Convex Hull is fast and calm. The explorer above shows the difference.

  2. Copy it down and turn it

    The viewport. Two short commands.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Shift+D, then Z, type -2.5, Enter. A copy drops straight down 2.5 m.
    2. b
      R, then Z, type 90, Enter. The copy turns a quarter turn and now threads through the first link edge-on.

    You should now see: two interlocked links. The Outliner lists Link and Link.001. Click Link.001 and look at the Physics tab: Rigid Body came along with the copy.

    Why type the numbers instead of dragging?

    Shift+D starts a move that follows the mouse. Pressing Z locks it to up-down and typing -2.5 makes every copy land exactly 2.5 m lower. Dragging would put the links at random spacings and the joints would not line up.

  3. Four more

    The viewport. The same two commands, four more times.

    Do this:

    1. a
      With the newest link selected: Shift+D, Z, -2.5, Enter, then R, Z, 90, Enter.
    2. b
      Repeat until the Outliner shows Link, Link.001, Link.002, Link.003, Link.004 and Link.005. Six in total.

    You should now see: a straight chain of six links from Z 18 down to Z 5.5, every link turned a quarter from its neighbours. Click the bottom one: the sidebar says Location Z 5.5 m.

    Six? The old sheet said six to ten.

    Six links and a ball make a pendulum about 15 m long, which swings slowly enough to look heavy and hits around frame 50. More links means a longer chain, a lower ball, and the wall has to move. Try it as an extension.

  4. The top link holds everything: Passive

    The Physics tab, F2.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the top link (Link). Physics tab › Type › Passive. The Mass box disappears: a Passive body never moves.
    2. b
      F2, type Anchor, Enter.

    You should now see: Anchor at the top of the Outliner list, Type Passive. The other five links are still Active.

    What if every link stayed Active?

    Press Space and the whole chain drops to the ground in a heap, because nothing is holding it. The old version of this lab had exactly this problem: every ring was Active and nothing was anchored.

End of Part 2. Save.

Part 3

The ball

Tools: Shift+S (snap), Add › Mesh › UV Sphere, Ctrl+J.

The ball needs an eye to hang from. Rather than build one, the bottom link becomes the eye: a sphere is placed just under it and the two are joined into one object called Ball. One object, one Rigid Body, no overlap problems.

  1. Put the cursor on the bottom link

    The viewport, then the Snap pie menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the bottom link, Link.005.
    2. b
      Hover the viewport and press Shift+S. A pie menu opens around the mouse. Click Cursor to Selected.

    You should now see: the red-and-white 3D cursor sits in the middle of the bottom link. Sidebar › View tab › 3D Cursor reads 0, 0, 5.5.

    What is the 3D cursor for?

    New objects appear at the cursor. Snapping it to a selected object is the quickest way to put a new object exactly where an old one is, without typing its numbers.

  2. A sphere, scaled and dropped under the link

    The Add menu, the sidebar, the right-click menu, the Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. It appears at the cursor, inside the bottom link.
    2. b
      Sidebar Scale: X 1.5, Y 1.5, Z 1.5 (a 3 m ball). Location Z: 2.8.
    3. c
      Right-click the sphere › Shade Smooth.
    4. d
      Material tab (red ball icon) › New › click the Base Color swatch › Hex › 161618. Metallic 0.8.

    You should now see: a dark metal ball hanging just under the bottom link, overlapping it a little, at Z 2.8.

    Why 2.8?

    The link’s origin is at 5.5 and the link is 3 m tall, so its bottom is at 4.0. The ball’s radius is 1.5, so a ball centred at 2.5 would just touch. 2.8 sinks it 0.3 m into the link so the two look attached. They never collide with each other once joined, so the overlap is harmless.

  3. Join them into Ball, mass 40

    The viewport, Ctrl+J, the Physics tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the sphere, then Shift-click the bottom link so the link is the active one (lighter orange).
    2. b
      Ctrl+J. One object. F2, type Ball, Enter.
    3. c
      Physics tab: Rigid Body is still there (it was the link’s). Mass: 40.

    You should now see: one object called Ball: the sphere and its eye link with one orange outline. Physics: Active, Mass 40 kg, Convex Hull.

    Why does the order of clicking matter?

    Ctrl+J keeps the active object (the last one clicked) and pours the others into it. Clicking the link last keeps the link’s Rigid Body, its name slot and its place in the chain. Click the sphere last and the joined object has no physics at all.

End of Part 3. Save.

Part 4

Ground and wall

Tools: Shift+C, the Physics tab again, the Bevel modifier, Shift+D along Y and Z.

The ground is a Passive plane. The wall is twenty copies of one Active block that already has its physics, its bevel and its colour, so you set everything once.

ObjectLoc XLoc YLoc ZRot XRot YRot ZScale XScale YScale ZPhysics
Torus → Link (then Anchor)0 m0 m18 m90°0°0°111Active, Mass 2; the top one Passive
Link.001 … Link.0050 m0 m15.5 … 5.5 m90°0°90°, 180°, -90°, 0°, 90°111copies, 2.5 m apart, each turned 90°
UV Sphere → joined into Ball0 m0 m2.8 m0°0°0°1.51.51.5Ball: Active, Mass 40
Plane → Ground0 m0 m0 m0°0°0°252525Passive
Cube → Block (× 20)3.5 m-4 … 4 m1 … 7 m0°0°0°111Active, Shape Box, Bevel 0.08
Camera-24 m-44 m12 m87°0°-29°111Focal Length 42

Blue cells are the ones you type. Grey cells stay at their default. The chain links are also rotated 50° around the Anchor in Step 16, which changes their numbers; that is expected.

  1. A ground that never moves

    The viewport, then the Physics tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport, press Shift+C: the cursor goes back to the world centre.
    2. b
      Add › Mesh › Plane, then S, type 25, Enter. F2, type Ground, Enter.
    3. c
      Physics tab › Rigid Body › Type: Passive.

    You should now see: a huge flat square under everything (from the front it is a line on the red X axis). Rigid Body: Passive. Do not tick Animated.

    Why Shift+C first?

    The cursor is still on the bottom link from Step 9. Without Shift+C the plane would appear 5.5 m up, cutting through the chain, and the blocks would fall straight through it. If that happened: click the plane, sidebar Location Z 0.

  2. One block, fully set up

    The sidebar, the Physics tab, the Modifiers (wrench) tab, the Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Cube. Sidebar Location: X 3.5, Y -4, Z 1. It sits on the ground, 2.5 m in front of the ball’s swing line.
    2. b
      Physics tab › Rigid Body. Type Active, Mass 1 kg. Shape: Box.
    3. c
      Wrench tab › Add Modifier › Generate › Bevel. Amount 0.08, Segments 2. (The edges catch the light, so you can see the blocks.)
    4. d
      Material tab › New › Base Color Hex C79E73. F2, type Block, Enter.

    You should now see: a sandy block with softly rounded edges at the near end of where the wall will be, Rigid Body Active, Shape Box.

    Why Box and not Convex Hull?

    For a cube they are the same shape, but Box is a single test for the physics engine while Convex Hull is eight corners to check. Twenty blocks, hundreds of frames: Box keeps it quick.

  3. Twenty blocks

    The viewport. Copies along Y, then rows up Z.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Shift+D, Y, type 2, Enter. A second block 2 m along. Do this four times in total: a row of five from Y -4 to Y 4.
    2. b
      Click the first block, Shift-click the other four: all five orange.
    3. c
      Shift+D, Z, type 2, Enter. A second row on top. Three times in total: four rows.

    You should now see: a wall five blocks wide and four high, 10 m by 8 m, standing on the ground at X 3.5. The Outliner runs Block to Block.019: twenty.

    Do the copies have physics?

    Yes: Shift+D copies the Rigid Body, the bevel and the material. Click any block and check the Physics tab if you like. That is why Step 13 set everything up before copying.

End of Part 4. Save.

Part 5

Raise it, join it, swing it

Tools: the Pivot Point, R Y, Object › Rigid Body › Connect, Space.

Three things turn the parts into a wrecking ball. The chain is rotated around the Anchor so the ball starts raised. Joints are made between neighbouring links so the chain holds together. Then Space: gravity does the rest.

How high, how fast, how soon

Drag the angle. The numbers are the same physics Blender runs.

  1. Pivot on the Anchor

    Front view. The Snap pie, then the Pivot Point dropdown in the viewport header.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Front view (Numpad 1). Click the Anchor.
    2. b
      Shift+S › Cursor to Selected. The cursor jumps up to the Anchor (Z 18).
    3. c
      Viewport header, middle: the Pivot Point dropdown (a small target icon). Pick 3D Cursor.

    You should now see: the cursor on the Anchor, and the pivot icon in the header now shows the cursor symbol.

    What does the pivot do?

    When you rotate several objects at once, Blender turns them around the pivot. Median Point (the default) is the middle of the selection, which would wreck the chain. 3D Cursor means “around here”, and the cursor is on the Anchor.

  2. Rotate the chain 50°

    The viewport. Select, then R.

    Predict first: The wall is on the right. Which way should the ball be raised so that it swings into the wall?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click Link.001, then Shift-click Link.002, Link.003, Link.004 and the Ball. Five selected. Not the Anchor, not the wall.
    2. b
      R, Y, type 50, Enter.

    You should now see: the chain tilted as one piece, still interlocked, with the ball raised to the left. Click the Ball: the sidebar shows Location X about -9.58, Z about 9.97.

    Why Y?

    In Front view the Y axis points straight at you, out of the screen. Rotating around it swings things left and right across the screen, like a clock hand. R X would tip the chain toward or away from you; R Z would spin it like a top.

  3. Connect: joints between the links

    The Object menu, then the Connect panel at the bottom-left of the viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Shift-click the Anchor as well. Six selected: Anchor, four links, Ball.
    2. b
      Object › Rigid Body › Connect.
    3. c
      Bottom-left of the viewport, a small Connect panel. Type: Point. Connection Pattern: Chain by Distance. Leave Pivot on Center. Do this before clicking anything else: the panel vanishes after your next action.

    You should now see: five small arrow-crosses where the links meet, and five new Constraint empties in the Outliner.

    What did that make?

    A Rigid Body Constraint is a joint between two objects. Point means a ball joint: the two can swing freely but cannot pull apart. Chain by Distance joins each object to its nearest neighbour, so Anchor–Link.001, Link.001–Link.002 and so on, down to Link.004–Ball. The joints are placed half-way between the origins, which is exactly where neighbouring links touch.

  4. Play it

    The viewport and the Timeline.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Orbit a little (middle-mouse drag) so you can see the wall face-on. Hover the viewport, press Space.
    2. b
      Watch: the chain swings down and through the bottom, and the ball hits the wall at about frame 50. Blocks fly.
    3. c
      Space pauses. Shift+← goes back to frame 1 and everything is back in place.
    4. d
      Header: Pivot Point back to Median Point, so later moves behave normally.

    You should now see: a swing, a hit, a mess. Then back to the raised pose at frame 1.

    The first play was slow. Normal?

    Yes. Blender simulates each frame the first time it reaches it and remembers the result in the cache. The second time through it just replays. Part 6 explains the cache and how to lock it.

End of Part 5. Save.

Part 6

Cache, camera, bake, render

Tools: the Timeline, the Scene tab, the camera Data tab, the Output tab.

Five seconds is enough. The camera gets exact numbers. Then the simulation is baked, which locks every frame so the render matches what you watched, and the movie is rendered as an .mp4.

The cache, hands on

Play fills it. Changing anything empties it. Bake locks it.

  1. Five seconds

    The Timeline along the bottom, then the Scene tab in the Properties editor.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Timeline: the End box, 120, Enter.
    2. b
      Properties › Scene tab (the cone-and-ball icon near the top of the column) › Rigid Body World › Cache › End: 120.

    You should now see: the timeline ruler runs 1 to 120, and the cache End reads 120.

    Two End boxes?

    The Timeline End is how long the film is. The cache End is how far Blender will simulate. If the cache stopped at 100 the ball would freeze mid-air for the last 20 frames. Matching them avoids that.

  2. Place the camera

    The Outliner, the sidebar, the green camera Data tab, Numpad 0.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click Camera in the Outliner. Sidebar Location: X -24, Y -44, Z 12. Rotation: X 87, Y 0, Z -29.
    2. b
      Properties › the green camera tab › Focal Length: 42.
    3. c
      Numpad 0 (or the camera icon under the gizmo): through the camera.

    You should now see: the whole chain at the left, the wall at the right, ground across the bottom, sky above. Checkpoint E shows the framing.

    Why those numbers?

    The camera stands 50 m away, front-left, 12 m up, turned 29° to the right to look along the swing and tilted down 3°. 42 mm is slightly wider than the default 50 mm so the 20 m chain fits with room to spare.

  3. Bake the simulation

    The Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Cache.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Cache › Bake. A progress bar runs through 120 frames.
    2. b
      Scrub the timeline (drag the blue marker): every frame is instant now. The button says Delete Bake.

    You should now see: Delete Bake where Bake was, and smooth scrubbing anywhere from 1 to 120.

    Why bake before rendering?

    Rendering evaluates the scene frame by frame in its own way. Without a bake, Blender may re-simulate during the render, and chaotic things like a chain can come out differently from what you watched: in testing, an unbaked render sent the ball clean over the wall. A bake is a locked recording; the render reads it. To change anything later: Delete Bake, change, play, Bake again.

  4. Render the movie and hand in

    The Output tab (printer icon), then the Render menu at the very top.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Output tab › Resolution %: 50.
    2. b
      Output panel › the path box: click the folder icon and pick your Physics labs folder. File Format: FFmpeg Video. Then Encoding › Container: MPEG-4.
    3. c
      Render › Render Animation (or Ctrl+F12). A window shows each frame rendering: a few minutes. Close it when it finishes.
    4. d
      Ctrl+S. Upload PhysicsLab1_WreckingBall_YourName.blend and the .mp4 (named 0001-0120.mp4) to SEQTA.

    You should now see: an .mp4 in your folder that plays the swing and the hit, and both files in SEQTA.

    Why 50%?

    Half-size frames render four times faster and still look fine on a screen. Set it back to 100% for a final version if there is time.

End of the lab.

Part 7

Finished early? Pick one

Tools: everything above, used again.

Each one is a small experiment. Remember the rule: Delete Bake, change one thing, play from frame 1, compare.

Change one number, predict first

Write down what you expect, then test: Ball Mass 5 instead of 40. Block Mass 5 instead of 1. Swing angle 25 instead of 50 (select the four links and the Ball, pivot on the cursor at the Anchor, R Y -25). Ground Friction 0.1 (Physics tab › Collisions › Surface Response). Which change stops the wall falling? Which makes the biggest mess?

A crane to hang it from

Add › Mesh › Cube, Location 0, 0, 18.5, Scale 0.3, 8, 0.3: a bar through the Anchor’s hole. Add a tall post at one end: Cube, Location 0, 9, 9.5, Scale 0.4, 0.4, 9.5. Give both a yellow material. No physics needed: the Anchor already does the holding. Make the bar Passive + Animated and keyframe it sliding along X and you have a moving crane that drags the chain.

A better wall

Real walls are laid in a running bond: every second row shifted half a block. Select rows 2 and 4 (ten blocks) and move them G Y 1. Now the ball has to break the bond. Or make smaller blocks: Scale 0.5 on the first block before copying, 1 m apart, ten wide and eight high (80 blocks; the bake takes longer).

A longer chain

Delete the Connect empties (select the five Constraints in the Outliner, X). Select the Ball, Shift+S › Cursor to Selected, then add two more links above the Ball the same way as Step 6 (copies of Link.004, Z -2.5 each, R Z 90), move the Ball down 5 m, move the wall to X 6, raise and Connect again. The pendulum is longer, so it swings slower and hits later: work out roughly when with the widget in Part 5 (the length is now about 20 m).

Slow motion

Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Speed 0.25. Delete Bake, play: everything happens at quarter speed, like a film replay. Set the Timeline End to 480 so the hit still fits, and the cache End too.

Something’s not right

Find the problem that matches yours.

I can’t orbit (no middle mouse button)

Drag on the coloured gizmo itself to orbit. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate 3 Button Mouse, then Alt + left-drag orbits.

The ring did not stretch into an oval

The selected vertices moved but not the right ones, or the move was not locked to Z. Ctrl+Z until the ring is round again. Then: Front view, Tab, Alt+Z (watch for the X-ray button lighting up), box from above-left to just above the middle, G then Z then 1 then Enter. If the oval leans, you pressed G and moved the mouse before Z.

The back of the ring stayed behind (a half-stretched, torn-looking link)

X-ray was off, so the box only caught the front vertices. Ctrl+Z, press Alt+Z, drag the box again. The X-ray button is the pair of overlapping squares at the top-right of the viewport.

I press Space and the whole chain falls in a heap

Nothing is holding it. Either the top link is still Active (click it, Physics tab, Type Passive) or you played before Step 17 made the joints. Shift+Left Arrow to go back to frame 1: everything returns.

The links fly apart, jitter or explode when I play

Either the links overlap and are colliding with each other because the joints do not exist yet (do Step 17), or the Connect panel was left on Fixed / Selected to Active (delete the Constraint empties in the Outliner and redo Step 17 with Point and Chain by Distance), or the chain was rotated AFTER connecting, so the joints are in the wrong place (delete the empties, keep the rotation, Connect again).

The Connect panel vanished before I set Point

It disappears after any other action. Press F9 with the mouse over the viewport to bring it back, or Ctrl+Z, select the six objects again and run Connect again.

The chain stretches like elastic or the ball hangs too low

Point joints are placed half-way between the origins of the two objects. If an origin is not in the middle of its link (Step 4 skipped on one link), the joint lands inside the metal and the links can pull apart. Select each link, Object › Set Origin › Origin to Geometry, then delete the empties and Connect again.

Blocks fall through the ground

Either the plane is Active (make it Passive) or it is not at Z 0 because the cursor was still on the chain when you added it. Click Ground, sidebar Location 0, 0, 0.

The wall collapses by itself before the ball arrives

Blocks overlapping each other. Each copy must be exactly 2 m apart (type the 2, do not drag), and their Shape must be Box. Also check Scale is 1, 1, 1 on the first block.

The ball swings but misses the wall

The wall is at X 3.5 and the ball swings along Y 0, so a block must sit at Y -4, -2, 0, 2 and 4. If your first block had a different Y, the row is in the wrong place. Or the chain was raised on the wrong side: the ball must start at negative X (to the left in Front view) so it swings toward +X.

R Y 50 scrambled the chain instead of tilting it

The pivot was still Median Point, so each link turned around the middle of the selection. Ctrl+Z, then Step 15: cursor on the Anchor, Pivot Point 3D Cursor, and rotate again.

The Physics tab is missing

Nothing is selected, or the selected thing is the camera or an empty. Click a mesh object (a link, the ball, a block) first. The tab is the blue orbit icon.

My copies have no Rigid Body

You duplicated before adding Rigid Body in Step 5. Select all the links (click one, Shift-click the rest), make sure the one WITH physics is active (click it last), then Object › Rigid Body › Copy from Active.

Playback is very slow

The first play simulates as it goes: normal. If every play is slow, the cache is being thrown away each time because something changes: a selected object being nudged, or the file is unsaved. Save, then Bake (Step 21).

Everything jumps back to the start when I click

That is frame 1: the raised pose. The simulation is only visible while the frame is past 1. Press Space or drag the timeline marker.

The render looks different from the viewport playback

The simulation was not baked, so the render re-simulated and took a different path. Delete Bake if there is one, play from frame 1, Bake, then render again.

The Mass box is greyed out or missing

The object is Passive (no mass needed) or Animated is ticked. Only the Anchor and Ground should be Passive.

Render Animation makes pictures, not a movie

File Format is still PNG. Output tab › File Format › FFmpeg Video, then Encoding › Container › MPEG-4, then render again.

The ball freezes in mid-air near the end

The cache End is shorter than the Timeline End. Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Cache › End 120, Delete Bake, play, Bake.

Eight quick questions

Pick an answer to lock it in. You’ll find out straight away whether you’re right.

1Which object should be Passive?

Right. Passive things never move; everything else is Active.

Not quite. Only the things that must never move are Passive: the Anchor (the hook) and the Ground.

2What does Alt+Z do in Step 3?

Right. Without X-ray the box only selects what you can see.

Not quite. Alt+Z toggles X-ray: see-through, so a box selects vertices at the back as well.

3Why does Step 5 add Rigid Body before Step 6 copies the link?

Right. Shift+D copies physics, modifiers and materials.

Not quite. Shift+D copies everything about an object, including its Rigid Body, so adding it first saves doing it six times.

4Why is the chain rotated around the Anchor with the pivot on the 3D cursor?

Right. Blender has no “let go”; frame 1 is the moment of release, so you pose it raised.

Not quite. The simulation starts from wherever things are at frame 1. Raising the chain around the Anchor is the only way to give the ball a swing.

5What does Object › Rigid Body › Connect with Type Point make?

Right. Chain by Distance joins each one to its nearest neighbour.

Not quite. Connect makes Rigid Body Constraints: with Type Point, ball joints that hold neighbours together while letting them swing.

6Why do the links use Convex Hull and not Mesh?

Right. A Mesh chain is famous for exploding; the joints do the holding instead.

Not quite. Mesh would be exact but thin tubes colliding make the simulation unstable. The joints hold the chain, so Convex Hull is fine and fast.

7Which change would make the ball hit later?

Right. A longer pendulum swings slower; the swing angle barely changes the timing.

Not quite. Pendulum timing depends on length, not mass or (much) the angle: a longer chain hits later.

8What does Bake do?

Right. Rendering reads the baked cache instead of re-simulating.

Not quite. Bake simulates all the frames and locks them, so scrubbing is instant and the render uses exactly those frames.

Check yourself

Tick each one you can honestly do now. Anything left unticked is what to ask about next lesson.

Think about it

A real wrecking ball weighs about 5 tonnes and the crane holds it still before dropping it. In our scene the ball is 40 kg and starts raised with no crane. Which of these differences matters for how the simulation looks, and which does not?

Upload to SEQTA — Physics Lab 1

Upload PhysicsLab1_WreckingBall_YourName.blend and your movie 0001-0120.mp4 (rename it PhysicsLab1_WreckingBall_YourName.mp4 if you like). The .blend should contain Anchor, four links, Ball, Ground, twenty blocks, five Constraint empties, a placed camera and a baked cache.

Due one week from when this lab was handed out.

Teacher notes

Timing

Two lessons. Lesson 1: Parts 1–4 (link, chain, ball, ground and wall). Lesson 2: Parts 5–6 (raise, connect, play, camera, bake, render) and extensions. The bake takes under a minute; the 120-frame render at 50% takes 2–5 minutes with EEVEE on a school machine.

What changed from the original sheet

  • The chain is anchored. The original made every ring Active and anchored nothing, so pressing Space dropped the whole chain in a heap. The top link is now Passive (Step 8).
  • The chain is held by Point constraints, not by Mesh collisions. The original’s core instruction (Shape › Mesh on every ring) was tested in Blender 5.2: a Mesh-collision torus chain is chaotic. Across small changes of swing angle it variously jammed, gained energy (the ball climbed higher than it started), or pulled apart entirely, and an unbaked render sent the ball over the wall. With Object › Rigid Body › Connect (Point, Chain by Distance) made after posing, the swing is repeatable: hit at frame 51–52, 15–18 of 20 blocks displaced, across every tested variation. Collision shapes are still taught (Part 2 card and explorer), with Mesh explained as “exact but twitchy”.
  • The ball is attached. The original added a UV sphere at the bottom ring’s centre with its own Rigid Body, so sphere and ring overlapped and the solver pushed them apart (its own note said “if the ball is too large it may pass through chain rings”). The sphere is now joined into the bottom link (Ctrl+J, link active) so Ball is one object with one Rigid Body.
  • Nothing swings by itself. The original never gave the ball any motion; it would simply hang. The chain is now rotated 50° around the Anchor (3D cursor as pivot) so frame 1 is the release.
  • Every object has numbers (table in Part 4) instead of “scale to wrecking-ball size” and “stack cubes in the path”. Link origins are centred (Origin to Geometry) so the Connect pivots land where the links touch.
  • Removed or corrected: “Ctrl+C then Ctrl+V to duplicate” (works, but Shift+D with typed offsets is the right tool); “R then X (or Y) to rotate the new ring 90°” (wrong axes for a standing ring: it is R Z); “tick Animated to anchor the plane” (Animated is for keyframed passive objects; Passive alone is correct); “File › Import › Wavefront OBJ” for blocks (unnecessary); “Switch to Viewport Shading mode” (not a thing). Added: X-ray for the box select, Shade Smooth, the cache and Bake, camera placement, and an .mp4 render instead of a screenshot.

Tested values

Every number, menu path and shortcut was checked by building the scene from these steps in Blender 5.2.2 (bpy) with the default solver (10 substeps, 10 iterations) and rendering the checkpoints and filmstrip from the baked file. Rigid body panel names, the Connect operator and its panel, the Snap pie and the Pivot Point dropdown are unchanged from Blender 4.2 LTS.

Where students usually get stuck

Box-selecting without X-ray (half the ring stays behind). Pressing Space before the Connect step (the chain explodes; Shift+Left fixes the view). Leaving the Connect panel on Fixed. Rotating with Median Point as pivot. Adding the ground plane while the cursor is still on the chain. Clicking the sphere last before Ctrl+J (the Ball loses its physics). Rendering without baking.

Quiz answers

1 Anchor and Ground. 2 X-ray. 3 Copies carry physics. 4 Raised start, gravity swings it. 5 Point joints between neighbours. 6 Calm and fast; joints hold the chain. 7 A longer chain. 8 Simulates and locks every frame.
